title: Macbeth: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth
specPoints: AO1: characters; AO2: methods of characterisation

tips.title: The murder is his idea first
tips.body: The witches say king hereafter; Macbeth supplies the horrid image. Say so in any answer on who is to blame.

tips.title: He decides against it
tips.body: We will proceed no further in this business, Act 1 Scene 7. The persuasion that follows is the hinge of the play.

tips.title: How she persuades
tips.body: Questions; manhood redefined; the baby; We fail?; a plan. The June 2024 mark scheme named her questions and her challenges to his masculinity.

tips.title: Two falls that cross
tips.body: He goes from conscience to supp'd full with horrors; she goes from unsex me here to Out, damned spot.

tips.title: Test the verdict
tips.body: Butcher and fiend-like queen is Malcolm's view from outside. The audience has seen more; say what, and you are exploring an interpretation.

why.matters: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth are the centre of almost every extract the exam can print, and the questions ask how far, how, and why: a judgement about people Shakespeare built to be judged in more than one way. Learning them as two lines of change, a conscience that dies and a will that breaks, gives every answer a spine and every extract a place on it. It also teaches something beyond the exam: that the verdict given on people at the end of their story is not the whole of what their story showed.

examples.title: The couple who push each other
examples.body: Stories about ambitious couples, in politics, business or crime, often divide the work the way Act 1 does: one partner doubts, the other drives. The interest is in what happens when the plan succeeds and the roles swap, which is the second half of *Macbeth*. The play is the pattern those stories still follow.

examples.title: The verdict and the view from inside
examples.body: News reports and history books give the verdict from outside, like Malcolm's. Biography, drama and a jury's full hearing give the view from inside. *Macbeth* gives its audience both and leaves them to weigh the difference, which is the skill a top-level answer shows.

steps.title: Macbeth before the murder: the soldier and the thought
steps.body:
Macbeth enters the play as a hero. A wounded soldier tells the king how he cut the rebel open “Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops”, and Duncan calls him “For brave Macbeth”. The violence that will destroy him is, at the start, what Scotland praises him for.

**The thought arrives at once.** Minutes after the witches hail him as king hereafter, he is shaken by an idea he does not name: the murder is a “Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair”, and “Present fears Are less than horrible imaginings” (Macbeth, 1.3). Nobody has suggested killing Duncan. The idea is his.

**Then he hides it.** He tells himself “If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me” (Macbeth, 1.3), and when Malcolm is named heir he turns to the dark: “Stars, hide your fires” (Macbeth, 1.4), “Let not light see my black and deep desires”. The first thing Macbeth does with his ambition is conceal it, and asides and soliloquies are how Shakespeare lets the audience see what the other characters cannot.

rows: Unseam'd him from the nave to the chops
A soldier whose violence is praised
The murder is his idea, unprompted
If chance will have me king
He hopes not to have to act
props.title: Macbeth in Act 1

visuals.alt: A table of four moments in Act 1 that show Macbeth before the murder, with what each shows

check.prompt: The witches say Macbeth will be king. Who first thinks of murder?
check.solution: Macbeth, in the asides of Act 1 Scene 3. The witches say only that he will be king; it is Macbeth whose hair stands on end at a horrid image he does not name. The letter is his, written to his wife, and she reads it in Act 1 Scene 5.

markScheme.description: Macbeth himself, in an aside minutes after the prophecy, before anyone has suggested it

options: Banquo, who urges him to act on the prophecy
Lady Macbeth, in her letter to Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 5, which he reads aloud to Banquo on the heath before they go to meet the king at Forres
The witches, who tell him to kill Duncan
Macbeth himself, in an aside minutes after the prophecy, before anyone has suggested it

steps.title: The soliloquy: a conscience at work
steps.body:
In Act 1 Scene 7, alone, Macbeth argues himself out of the murder. The speech opens “If it were done when ’tis done, then ’twere well It were done quickly” (Macbeth, 1.7), a sentence that circles the deed without naming it.

**His reasons are good ones.** Duncan is his king, his kinsman and his guest; Duncan has been a good king, and his virtues “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued” against his murder. The images are of heaven and judgement.

**And he knows his motive.** “I have no spur” (Macbeth, 1.7) to prick the sides of his intent, only “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” (Macbeth, 1.7). He names his own flaw.

**He decides.** When his wife enters he tells her “We will proceed no further in this business” (Macbeth, 1.7). The play gives its hero a clear moral choice and lets him make the right one, so that everything after is a choice to unmake it.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on Macbeth's case against the murder in Act 1 Scene 7: loyalty, hospitality, Duncan's virtue, and his own motive, ambition

check.prompt: What does the image of vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself, suggest about Macbeth?
check.solution: The image is of a rider who vaults so hard into the saddle that he goes over the other side. Macbeth names his only motive and sees where it leads. That self-knowledge is what makes him tragic: he does the murder knowing what it is.

markScheme.description: He sees his ambition as a rider leaping too far and falling, so he knows the flaw that will ruin him

options: He sees his ambition as a rider leaping too far and falling, so he knows the flaw that will ruin him
He is thinking of a horse race he has watched
He believes his ambition is a strength that will carry him safely over every obstacle, as a good horse carries a rider over a fence, and he is confident of success
He has no ambition, only loyalty

steps.title: Lady Macbeth: the letter and the spirits
steps.body:
Lady Macbeth enters reading her husband's letter about the witches, and her first thought is that he is not ruthless enough. His nature is “too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness” (Lady Macbeth, 1.5); he is “Art not without ambition, but without The illness should attend it”.

**She calls on spirits.** When she hears that Duncan will stay the night, she asks the spirits that tend on mortal thoughts to “unsex me here” (Lady Macbeth, 1.5), to fill her with cruelty, and to “And take my milk for gall”. Then “Come, thick night” (Lady Macbeth, 1.5). The words are an invocation: in a play written for an audience that believed in witchcraft, a woman calling on spirits is doing something dangerous, not speaking in metaphor.

**She plans the deception.** She greets Macbeth with his new titles, reads his face at once, “Your face, my thane, is as a book” (Lady Macbeth, 1.5), and tells him how to hide it: “look like the innocent flower, But be the serpent under’t” (Lady Macbeth, 1.5).

rows: She asks to lose what she thinks is womanly
props.title: Lady Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 5

visuals.alt: A table of four lines from Lady Macbeth's first scene, with what each shows about her

check.prompt: Why does Lady Macbeth ask the spirits to unsex me here?
check.solution: She asks to be filled with cruelty in place of the pity and remorse she associates with being a woman, and to have her milk taken for gall. The line assumes that tenderness is womanly; her collapse in Act 5 suggests the spirits could not take it away.

markScheme.description: She believes that pity and gentleness belong to her as a woman, and asks to be rid of them so she can act

options: She is asking to be protected from Duncan
She believes that pity and gentleness belong to her as a woman, and asks to be rid of them so she can act
She wants the spirits to make Macbeth kinder
She wants to become a man so that she can become king herself after Duncan is dead, since the witches have promised the crown to her rather than to her husband

steps.title: The persuasion: Act 1 Scene 7
steps.body: The June 2024 extract was this conversation, and the question asked how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character. The indicative content in the mark scheme picked out her repeated questions to Macbeth and her challenges to his masculinity, and her use of extreme images to persuade him. Here is how the conversation works.

visuals.problem: How does Lady Macbeth change her husband's mind in Act 1 Scene 7?

steps.text: She attacks with questions: “Was the hope drunk Wherein you dress’d yourself?” “Art thou afeard” to be the same in act as in desire?
steps.note: Questions he cannot answer without shame: his hope was drunk, and he is a coward.

steps.text: He defends himself: “I dare do all that may become a man”.
steps.note: A true definition of manhood, with limits. She will change the definition.

steps.text: She redefines what a man is: “When you durst do it, then you were a man” (Lady Macbeth, 1.7).
steps.note: Manhood becomes daring. On her terms, refusing is unmanly.

steps.text: She uses an extreme image: “I have given suck”, and she would have dashed the brains out of her smiling baby had she sworn to it, as he has sworn to this.
steps.note: The most shocking thing she can imagine, used as a measure of how binding a promise is.

steps.text: He asks what if they fail. She answers “We fail?”, then “screw your courage to the sticking-place” (Lady Macbeth, 1.7), and gives him the plan.
steps.note: A question answered with a question, then a practical plan: the drugged grooms.

steps.text: He is won: “Bring forth men-children only” (Macbeth, 1.7), and “False face must hide what the false heart doth know” (Macbeth, 1.7).
steps.note: He praises her as a mother of soldiers and takes on her language of the false face.

rows: He must answer or feel shamed
props.title: How she persuades him

visuals.alt: A table of Lady Macbeth's four methods of persuasion in Act 1 Scene 7 with the effect of each

check.prompt: How does Lady Macbeth use the word man against Macbeth in Act 1 Scene 7?
check.solution: Macbeth says he dares do all that may become a man; she answers that when he dared to do it, then he was a man. The argument is about the meaning of one word, and she wins it by changing the meaning. The mark scheme's indicative content for June 2024 names her challenges to his masculinity.

markScheme.description: She redefines manhood as daring to act, so that refusing the murder makes him less of a man

options: She never mentions manhood
She reminds him that a man must be loyal to his king and his guest, as he himself argued in his soliloquy only a few lines earlier, and agrees they should stop
She redefines manhood as daring to act, so that refusing the murder makes him less of a man
She says that she is more of a man than he is and will do the murder herself

steps.title: After the murder: the marriage turns
steps.body:
**Act 2: she is in control.** Macbeth comes back unable to stop talking about a voice that cried sleep no more; “I am afraid to think what I have done” (Macbeth, 2.2). She calls him “Infirm of purpose”, takes the daggers back herself, and returns with bloody hands: “My hands are of your color, but I shame To wear a heart so white” (Lady Macbeth, 2.2). Yet she has already admitted a limit: “Had he not resembled My father as he slept, I had done’t” (Lady Macbeth, 2.2).

**Act 3: he shuts her out.** He plans Banquo's murder without her: “Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck” (Macbeth, 3.2). She is not at peace either: alone, she says “Naught’s had, all’s spent” (Lady Macbeth, 3.2); to him, “what’s done is done”. At the banquet she covers for him in front of the lords and taunts him once more, “Are you a man?” (Lady Macbeth, 3.4), but her power over him has gone.

**Act 5: apart.** She walks in her sleep; he prepares for battle. When he is told “The Queen, my lord, is dead” (Seyton, 5.5), he says “She should have died hereafter” (Macbeth, 5.5). The pair who planned together in Act 1 end the play without a word to each other.

rows: Screw your courage to the sticking-place
A little water clears us of this deed
Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck
props.title: The marriage, act by act

visuals.alt: A table of who leads in the marriage act by act, with a line from each act

check.prompt: What does Macbeth's line Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck show about the marriage in Act 3?
check.solution: In Act 1 she planned and he followed. In Act 3 he plans Banquo's murder and tells her nothing, with an endearment. The line can be read as care, but the change it marks is in power: the partnership of Act 1 is over, and she is on the outside.

markScheme.description: He now plans murders without her, and the tender name hides the fact that he has shut her out

options: He is protecting her because he still loves her deeply and does not want her troubled by the plan to kill Banquo, which shows that the marriage is stronger than it was in Act 1
She has refused to help him any more
He is joking with her before the banquet
He now plans murders without her, and the tender name hides the fact that he has shut her out

steps.title: Two falls: the mind that sees and the mind that breaks
steps.body:
**Macbeth hardens.** After Duncan he cannot say Amen, and “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood” (Macbeth, 2.2). By Act 3 “O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife” (Macbeth, 3.2). Then the killing becomes easier: “I am in blood Stepp’d in so far” (Macbeth, 3.4). By Act 5 he feels almost nothing: “I have supp’d full with horrors” (Macbeth, 5.5); “I have liv’d long enough” (Macbeth, 5.3); his life has fallen into “the sere, the yellow leaf”. And he dies fighting: “I’ll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack’d” (Macbeth, 5.3); “lay on, Macduff” (Macbeth, 5.8).

**Lady Macbeth breaks.** The woman who said a little water would clear them walks at night trying to wash her hands: “Out, damned spot” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1); “who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1); “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand” (Lady Macbeth, 5.1). The doctor says “More needs she the divine than the physician” (the Doctor, 5.1). She dies off stage, by her own hand as it is thought; Malcolm says she took her life “by self and violent hands”.

They cross. In Act 1 he had the conscience and she had the will. By Act 5 she is destroyed by the conscience she called on spirits to remove, and he has become the thing she asked to be.

visuals.alt: A table comparing the falls of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth act by act: he moves from conscience to numbness, she from will to breakdown

check.prompt: In what sense do Macbeth and Lady Macbeth swap places over the play?
check.solution: In Act 1 he argues against the murder and she overrules him. By Act 5 he has supped full with horrors and feels almost nothing, while she walks at night washing hands that cannot be cleaned. The crossing is a structure Shakespeare builds from their own lines.

markScheme.description: He begins with the conscience and ends numb; she begins with the will and ends destroyed by guilt

options: He begins with the conscience and ends numb; she begins with the will and ends destroyed by guilt
He begins as king and ends as thane, while she begins as a servant and ends as queen, so their social positions are exactly reversed by the time the play is over
They do not change: he is always weak and she is always strong
She becomes the murderer of Banquo and he becomes the sleepwalker

steps.title: How far is Lady Macbeth strong?
steps.body:
Take the June 2024 question: *Starting with this conversation, explore how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character.* The words *how far* ask for a judgement, not a list.

Plan an answer in five lines:

1. The idea: where her strength comes from and where it runs out.
2. Two methods in the Act 1 Scene 7 conversation that show strength, with a line each.
3. One moment elsewhere where she is still strong: the daggers in Act 2, or the banquet in Act 3.
4. One moment where the strength fails: the father she could not kill, or the sleepwalking.
5. One sentence of context tied to a line: what her audience expected of a wife and a mother.

Then write the paragraph that turns: the one where strength becomes its limit.

boxes.title: Strong
boxes.body: Questions, manhood redefined, the extreme image

boxes.title: Its limit
boxes.body: Had he not resembled my father

boxes.title: Broken
boxes.body: Out, damned spot; by self and violent hands

visuals.alt: Four boxes planning a how-far answer on Lady Macbeth: where she is strong, where she is still strong, the limit, and the breakdown

check.prompt: Which moment is the best evidence that Lady Macbeth's strength had a limit even before the sleepwalking?
check.solution: In Act 2 she admits that she went to do the murder and could not, because the sleeping king looked like her father. It is a limit she reveals in the middle of her strongest scene. The other lines show her will; this one shows where it stopped.

markScheme.description: Had he not resembled my father as he slept, I had done't: she could not kill Duncan herself

options: Look like the innocent flower: she tells Macbeth to hide
Had he not resembled my father as he slept, I had done't: she could not kill Duncan herself
Screw your courage to the sticking-place: she insists that the plan cannot fail if Macbeth is brave enough to carry it through, and that she will make sure of it herself
Unsex me here: she asks spirits to fill her with cruelty

steps.title: Interpretations: butcher and fiend-like queen?
steps.body:
The last words about them are Malcolm's: “this dead butcher, and his fiend-like queen” (Malcolm, 5.8). A top-level answer tests that verdict instead of repeating it.

**Macbeth: a butcher, or a tragic hero?** The verdict fits the man who kills a family that threatens nothing. It does not fit the man who argued against the first murder, who knew his motive was only vaulting ambition, and whose despair in the tomorrow speech is some of the most moving verse in the play. Shakespeare makes the audience hold both.

**Lady Macbeth: fiend-like?** She called on spirits and imagined killing her baby. She also could not kill a man who looked like her father, fainted or seemed to faint when the murder was discovered, and was broken by guilt. Malcolm never sees her sleepwalk; the audience does. The play gives its audience more than it gives Malcolm.

**How to write it.** Quote the verdict, then test it: *Malcolm's fiend-like queen is the view from outside; the sleepwalking scene is the view from inside, and only the audience has both.* That is an interpretation explored, which the Level 6 descriptor asks for.

visuals.alt: Four boxes testing Malcolm's verdict on Macbeth as a butcher and Lady Macbeth as fiend-like, with evidence for and against each

check.prompt: Which sentence explores Malcolm's verdict of this dead butcher, and his fiend-like queen in the way the top level rewards?
check.solution: The top level asks for exploration of interpretations. Testing the verdict against what the audience has seen and Malcolm has not does that. Agreeing with a list of crimes, blaming the witches without evidence, or placing the line are all lower-level moves.

markScheme.description: Malcolm's verdict is the view from outside; the audience has seen the conscience and the sleepwalking he never saw, so it cannot fully agree

options: Malcolm says this at the end of the play
Malcolm is right, because Macbeth killed Duncan, Banquo and the family of Macduff, and Lady Macbeth helped him to kill Duncan, so they are both evil and deserve to be called a butcher and a fiend
Malcolm's verdict is the view from outside; the audience has seen the conscience and the sleepwalking he never saw, so it cannot fully agree
Malcolm is wrong, because Macbeth and Lady Macbeth were victims of the witches

steps.title: Macbeth and Lady Macbeth in one page
steps.body:
A hero with a conscience and a wife with a will; a persuasion that works; a marriage that turns; two falls that cross.

- **Macbeth before the murder:** the praised soldier; the horrid image that is his own idea; Stars, hide your fires; the soliloquy that names vaulting ambition and decides against.
- **Lady Macbeth in Act 1:** the milk of human kindness; unsex me here; the innocent flower and the serpent.
- **The persuasion:** questions, manhood redefined, the baby, We fail?, the plan.
- **The marriage:** she leads in Acts 1 and 2; he shuts her out in Act 3; they are apart in Act 5.
- **The falls:** he hardens to supp'd full with horrors; she breaks to Out, damned spot.
- **The verdict:** butcher and fiend-like queen, tested against what only the audience has seen.

visuals.alt: A summary table of Macbeth and Lady Macbeth: how each starts, a key line, and how each ends

check.prompt: Which character says Out, damned spot?
check.solution: Lady Macbeth, walking in her sleep in Act 5 Scene 1 and trying to wash the blood she believes is still on her hands. It answers her own line of Act 2, A little water clears us of this deed.

markScheme.description: Lady Macbeth

questions.prompt: Why does Lady Macbeth fear her husband's nature when she reads his letter?
questions.solution: She says he is not without ambition but is too full of the milk of human kindness to catch the nearest way. The image of milk returns when she asks the spirits to take her own milk for gall.

markScheme.description: It is too full o' th' milk of human kindness to take the quickest way to the crown

options: It is too full o' th' milk of human kindness to take the quickest way to the crown
He believes the witches too readily
He has no ambition at all and will refuse the crown if it is offered to him, because he is loyal to Duncan and would rather remain a soldier than become a king
He is too cruel and will frighten the king

questions.prompt: Complete Lady Macbeth's instruction to Macbeth: look like the innocent flower, but be the ... under't.
questions.solution: Serpent. The image recalls the serpent in the Garden of Eden, which deceived Eve; a Jacobean audience would hear the fall of man behind it. It is the plan in one line: an innocent surface over a deadly purpose.

markScheme.description: serpent

questions.prompt: What reasons against the murder does Macbeth give in his soliloquy in Act 1 Scene 7?
questions.solution: He sets out a double trust: he is Duncan's kinsman and subject, and his host, who should shut the door against the murderer rather than bear the knife himself. Duncan's virtues would plead like angels, trumpet-tongued. The reasons are moral, and he finds only ambition on the other side.

markScheme.description: Duncan is his king, kinsman and guest, and so good a king his virtues will plead like angels

options: Banquo has warned him not to do it
Duncan is his king, kinsman and guest, and so good a king his virtues will plead like angels
He is afraid of being caught by the grooms, and he does not think his wife will support him if the plan goes wrong, so he would rather wait for chance to crown him
He does not want to be king

questions.prompt: Why can't Lady Macbeth kill Duncan herself?
questions.solution: She says Had he not resembled my father as he slept, I had done't. The admission comes in the middle of the scene where she seems strongest, and it is the first sign of the limit that the sleepwalking will expose.

markScheme.description: He resembled her father as he slept

options: The grooms woke up before she could reach the king's chamber, and she heard Macbeth coming up the stairs and was afraid of being seen by him before the deed was done
She had given the daggers to Macbeth already
He resembled her father as he slept
She was afraid of the witches

questions.prompt: Put these lines of Lady Macbeth in the order the play presents them.
questions.solution: Act 1 Scene 5, Act 1 Scene 7, Act 2 Scene 2, Act 3 Scene 4, Act 5 Scene 1. Read in order, the lines trace her from confidence to breakdown.

markScheme.description: the five lines in order

items: Screw your courage to the sticking-place
A little water clears us of this deed

questions.prompt: What does Macbeth mean by I am in blood stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more, returning were as tedious as go o'er?
questions.solution: The image is of a man halfway across a river of blood: turning back is no easier than going on. It is a decision to continue, spoken after the banquet, and it marks the point where murder becomes a habit rather than a choice.

markScheme.description: He has killed so much that going back would be as hard as going on, so he will go on

options: He has been wounded in the battle and is bleeding so heavily that he cannot walk back to the castle, and must be carried across the river to safety by his soldiers
He wants to stop killing and return to how he was
He is describing the moat around Dunsinane
He has killed so much that going back would be as hard as going on, so he will go on

questions.prompt: Macbeth says his mind is full of what, in Act 3?
questions.solution: Scorpions: O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife. The image is of a mind that stings itself. He is king, and has no peace.

markScheme.description: scorpions

questions.prompt: How does Macbeth react when he is told that the Queen is dead?
questions.solution: She should have died hereafter, followed by Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, and a life that is a tale told by an idiot, signifying nothing. The flatness is the point: the man who once could not stop thinking about blood can no longer feel his wife's death.

markScheme.description: She should have died hereafter, and then the tomorrow speech: life seems meaningless to him

options: She should have died hereafter, and then the tomorrow speech: life seems meaningless to him
He weeps, calls for the doctor, and orders that the battle be delayed so that she can be buried at Scone with the honours of a queen, which shows how much he still loves her
He blames the witches and swears revenge on them
He does not hear the news because the battle has begun

questions.prompt: Which line shows Macbeth adopting his wife's language of deception after she has persuaded him?
questions.solution: False face must hide what the false heart doth know ends Act 1: her innocent flower and serpent, in his mouth. It shows the persuasion has worked on his words as well as his plan.

markScheme.description: False face must hide what the false heart doth know

options: I have no spur to prick the sides of my intent
False face must hide what the false heart doth know
So foul and fair a day I have not seen
Is this a dagger which I see before me, the handle toward my hand? Come, let me clutch thee: I have thee not, and yet I see thee still

questions.prompt: The mark scheme for June 2024 suggested that answers might comment on Lady Macbeth's lack of strength in one scene. Which scene?
questions.solution: The indicative content lists comments on Lady Macbeth's lack of strength in the sleepwalking scene, and her resolve or strength in the banquet scene. It is a list of what answers might include, not a required set of points.

markScheme.description: The sleepwalking scene

options: The banquet scene, where the lords see her faint when Banquo's ghost appears and she has to be carried from the hall by her attendants
The scene where she reads the letter
The sleepwalking scene
The conversation in Act 1 Scene 7

questions.prompt: What does Lady Macbeth's Naught's had, all's spent, spoken alone in Act 3, show?
questions.solution: Spoken alone, the line is the first sign that she, too, is suffering: desire is got without content. To Macbeth she says what's done is done. The gap between what she says alone and what she says to him is a method: the audience sees what her husband cannot.

markScheme.description: They have what they wanted and no content in it: the crown has brought no peace

options: She wants Macbeth to kill Banquo
She is pleased with how things have gone
She has spent all the money in the royal treasury on the coronation feast, and must ask Macbeth to raise taxes on the thanes before the banquet can be paid for
They have what they wanted and no content in it: the crown has brought no peace

questions.prompt: How does the image of Lady Macbeth's milk develop across Act 1?
questions.solution: Milk is kindness in Macbeth, nourishment turned to poison in her invocation, and motherhood used as a weapon in the persuasion. The image connects what she asks to become with what she will not be able to escape.

markScheme.description: Macbeth is too full of the milk of human kindness; she asks for her milk to be taken for gall; she has given suck

options: Macbeth is too full of the milk of human kindness; she asks for her milk to be taken for gall; she has given suck
Macbeth calls her a mother of milk
She tells Macbeth that the milk served at the feast has been poisoned, and that the grooms who drink it will sleep so soundly that they will not wake when he enters Duncan's chamber
Milk is mentioned only once

questions.prompt: In Act 5 who, besides a gentlewoman, watches Lady Macbeth walk in her sleep?
questions.solution: A doctor, who concludes that More needs she the divine than the physician: her illness is of the soul, and a priest would help her more than he can.

markScheme.description: the doctor

questions.prompt: Put these lines of Macbeth in the order the play presents them, from conscience to despair.
questions.solution: Act 1 Scene 7, Act 2 Scene 2, Act 3 Scene 2, Act 5 Scene 5. The decision against, the horror of blood, the stinging mind, and at last numbness.

items: We will proceed no further in this business

O, full of scorpions is my mind, dear wife

questions.prompt: Starting with the conversation in Act 1 Scene 7, explore how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character. Write the opening idea and two paragraphs: one on the conversation, and one on the play as a whole that shows where her strength ends.
questions.solution: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as strong in will and in words, and shows that the strength was borrowed from spirits she could not keep. In the conversation she wins by questions and definitions. “Was the hope drunk Wherein you dress’d yourself?” and “Art thou afeard” leave Macbeth nothing to answer without shame, and when he defends a limited manhood, “I dare do all that may become a man”, she changes the meaning of the word: “When you durst do it, then you were a man”. Her most extreme image, “I have given suck” and would have dashed the brains out of her smiling child, turns motherhood, the thing a Jacobean audience expected a wife to be defined by, into a measure of how binding a promise is, and her answer to his fear, “We fail?”, is a question that makes failure unthinkable. Yet the play shows where that strength stops. In Act 2 she admits she could not kill the king herself: “Had he not resembled My father as he slept, I had done’t”. The tenderness she asked the spirits to take away was still there, and by Act 5 it has come back as guilt: “Out, damned spot”, and “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”. The woman who told her husband that “A little water clears us of this deed” cannot now clean her own hand, and she dies, as Malcolm reports, “by self and violent hands”. She is strong for as long as the deed is a plan; once it is a memory, the strength is gone.

questions.modelAnswer: Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as strong in will and in words, and shows that the strength was borrowed from spirits she could not keep. In the conversation she wins by questions and definitions. “Was the hope drunk Wherein you dress’d yourself?” and “Art thou afeard” leave Macbeth nothing to answer without shame, and when he defends a limited manhood, “I dare do all that may become a man”, she changes the meaning of the word: “When you durst do it, then you were a man”. Her most extreme image, “I have given suck” and would have dashed the brains out of her smiling child, turns motherhood, the thing a Jacobean audience expected a wife to be defined by, into a measure of how binding a promise is, and her answer to his fear, “We fail?”, is a question that makes failure unthinkable. Yet the play shows where that strength stops. In Act 2 she admits she could not kill the king herself: “Had he not resembled My father as he slept, I had done’t”. The tenderness she asked the spirits to take away was still there, and by Act 5 it has come back as guilt: “Out, damned spot”, and “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand”. The woman who told her husband that “A little water clears us of this deed” cannot now clean her own hand, and she dies, as Malcolm reports, “by self and violent hands”. She is strong for as long as the deed is a plan; once it is a memory, the strength is gone.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Shakespeare presents Macbeth's conscience in Act 1, and one on how he presents its loss by Act 5.
questions.solution:
In Act 1 Shakespeare gives Macbeth a conscience that argues in images of heaven. Alone in Act 1 Scene 7, he circles the deed without naming it, “If it were done when ’tis done, then ’twere well It were done quickly”, and finds every reason against it: Duncan's virtues “Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued”, while on his own side he has “I have no spur” but “Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself”. He names his flaw exactly and decides, “We will proceed no further in this business”. The soliloquy form lets the audience hear a man choose right before he chooses wrong.

By Act 5 the conscience has not been defeated so much as worn out. “I have supp’d full with horrors”, he says, and his life has fallen into “the sere, the yellow leaf”. When he hears that his wife is dead he can only answer “She should have died hereafter” and turn to “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow”, a life that is “a tale Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, Signifying nothing”. The man who once could not stop seeing blood now feels nothing, and the change is what makes him tragic rather than simply wicked: Shakespeare lets the audience watch a conscience die, and the last flash of the soldier, “lay on, Macduff”, is the only feeling left.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "Lady Macbeth is evil from start to finish." What is the better account?
questions.solution: The evidence for cruelty is real, and the evidence against is in her own words: the father she could not kill, Naught's had, all's spent, and the sleepwalking. A how-far judgement weighs both.

markScheme.description: She wills herself to cruelty, but cannot kill a man like her father and is broken by guilt, so the play shows a limit

questions.prompt: Why is it significant that Malcolm never sees Lady Macbeth sleepwalk?
questions.solution: Only the doctor and the gentlewoman see the sleepwalking, and they keep it secret. Malcolm's verdict is made from outside, on the evidence of her crimes. The audience has more evidence, and that gap is where an interpretation can be explored.

markScheme.description: The audience has seen her guilt and he has not, so his fiend-like queen is a verdict the audience can test

options: Because Malcolm is in England throughout Act 5 and never returns to Scotland, so he cannot become king until the doctor sends him a report on the queen's health and the lords invite him back
Because the sleepwalking happens after the play ends

examTechnique.body:
**How far means judge.** A question like June 2024's, how far Shakespeare presents Lady Macbeth as a strong female character, wants an argument with a turn: where the strength is and where it ends.

**Start in the extract.** Name her or his methods there: questions, redefinitions, images, asides, soliloquy.

**Move out with the line of change.** For Macbeth, from the soliloquy of Act 1 Scene 7 to supp'd full with horrors; for Lady Macbeth, from unsex me here to Out, damned spot.

**Test the verdict.** Butcher and fiend-like queen is a view, not a fact; one sentence on what the audience knows and Malcolm does not is interpretation.
examinerErrors: Blaming the witches for the murder, when the horrid image is Macbeth's own.
Writing that Lady Macbeth is simply evil, without the father she could not kill or the sleepwalking.
Listing quotations about a character without the change across the play.
Answering how far with only one side.
Misquoting the famous lines: learn them exactly.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the two characters as lines of change that cross, and it answers how far with a judgement that turns. In the extract it names the methods of persuasion or of self-revelation; out of it, it chooses the moment where the line bends, the father Lady Macbeth could not kill or the conscience that becomes supp'd full with horrors. It quotes exactly and briefly, ties context to a line, and tests Malcolm's verdict against what only the audience has seen.
